passage:
Greenhill Summer Festival: Saturday 12 July, 11 a.m.–9 p.m., Greenhill Park

A  Food and market. Over forty stalls will sell food from around the world, along with crafts, plants and second-hand books. Please bring your own cup or bottle, as the festival is aiming to be free of single-use plastic this year. Free drinking water is available at the tap next to the bandstand.

B  Music. Local bands and choirs will perform on the main stage throughout the afternoon. In the evening, from 7 p.m., the headline act, a twelve-piece band playing music from West Africa and the Caribbean, will close the festival.

C  Children's area. Activities include face painting, a storytelling tent and a small climbing wall (children must be at least six years old to use the wall). All activities in the children's area are free. Children under twelve must be supervised by an adult at all times.

D  Getting there. Parking near the park is very limited, so please walk, cycle or use public transport if possible. Extra buses will run on route 14 between the railway station and the park gates. Secure bicycle parking is available at the north entrance.

E  Weather. The festival will go ahead whatever the weather, but some activities may be moved indoors to the community hall if there is heavy rain. Updates will be posted on the festival's social media pages on the morning of the event.

passage:
Volunteers Wanted for the Harbour Lights Festival

A  The Harbour Lights Festival returns this October for its tenth year, with three evenings of lantern parades, outdoor theatre and live music along the waterfront. The festival is run almost entirely by volunteers, and we need around 150 people to help it run smoothly.

B  There are many different roles available. Stewards help guide crowds, answer visitors' questions and make sure that paths and exits are kept clear. Lantern workshop assistants help children and families make paper lanterns in the weeks before the festival. Information point volunteers hand out programmes and maps, while a small team of photographers records the event for our archive.

C  No previous experience is necessary for most roles, but stewards must be at least eighteen and must attend a two-hour training session on the Saturday before the festival. Volunteers are asked to commit to at least one four-hour shift, and they can choose the shifts that suit them when they register.

D  In return, all volunteers will receive a festival T-shirt, a meal voucher for each shift and an invitation to the thank-you party in November. Volunteering is also a great way to meet people and gain experience that can be included in a CV. To register, complete the form at the community centre or online by 15 September.

explanation: 第A段落に今年で10年目とあるので TRUE。

passage:
Two Wheels: How the Bicycle Changed Everyday Life

A  The bicycle is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a relatively recent invention. The first machine with two wheels in line, built in Germany in 1817, had no pedals at all. Riders sat on a wooden frame and pushed themselves along with their feet. Although it caused a brief fashion among wealthy young men, it was heavy, uncomfortable and difficult to steer, and interest soon faded.

B  In the 1860s, French makers attached pedals directly to the front wheel, creating a machine that became known in English as the 'boneshaker' because of its iron tyres and rough ride on cobbled streets. Since each turn of the pedals produced one turn of the wheel, makers soon realised that a larger front wheel would allow the rider to travel further with every revolution. This led to the high-wheeled bicycle of the 1870s, with a front wheel that could be more than a metre and a half in diameter. It was fast, but it was also dangerous: riders sat high above the ground and could easily be thrown forward over the handlebars.

C  The solution came in the 1880s with the so-called 'safety bicycle'. It had two wheels of similar size and was driven by a chain connecting the pedals to the rear wheel, so that speed no longer depended on the size of the wheel. Soon afterwards, the introduction of air-filled rubber tyres made riding far more comfortable. The basic design of the safety bicycle has changed remarkably little since then.

D  The result was a cycling boom in the 1890s. For the first time, large numbers of ordinary people had access to an affordable means of personal transport that could carry them further than they could walk. Workers could live further from factories, and young people from different villages met more easily. The bicycle also played an important part in changing attitudes towards women's independence. Women who cycled gained a new freedom of movement, and the practical need to ride comfortably encouraged a move away from long, heavy skirts and tight clothing.

E  In the twentieth century, the spread of the motor car pushed cycling to the margins in many countries, although it remained a major form of transport in parts of Asia and in a few European countries. Today, concerns about traffic congestion, air pollution and health have brought renewed interest. Many cities are building separate cycle lanes and introducing bicycle-sharing schemes, while electric bicycles are making longer journeys and hilly routes accessible to people who might not otherwise cycle. Two centuries after its invention, the bicycle may be entering a new golden age.

passage:
The Rise of the Shared Office

A  Not long ago, most office workers had a desk in a building owned or rented by their employer, while freelancers and people running small businesses usually worked from home or in cafés. In the past two decades, a third option has become increasingly popular: the co-working space, a shared office in which people from different organisations rent desks or small rooms, often on a monthly or even daily basis.

B  Co-working spaces typically provide fast internet, printers, meeting rooms and kitchens, as well as the less tangible benefit of company. Many people who work from home report feeling isolated, and surveys of co-working members frequently mention the opportunity to meet other people as one of the main reasons for joining. Some spaces actively encourage members to get to know one another by organising lunches, talks and workshops, hoping that useful professional connections will result.

C  Flexibility is another major attraction. A conventional office lease may require a company to commit to a space for several years, which is risky for a new business whose size may change rapidly. In a co-working space, a business can rent two desks one month and ten the next. Increasingly, large companies also use co-working spaces, for example to house small project teams or to give staff who live far from the main office somewhere to work closer to home.

D  The rapid expansion of remote working since 2020 has had mixed effects on the industry. On the one hand, many employees discovered that they did not need to be in a central office every day, and some companies reduced their office space as a result. On the other hand, many people found that working at home every day had disadvantages, such as distractions and the difficulty of separating work from private life. Co-working spaces in suburbs and small towns, close to where people live, have benefited from this trend.

E  Co-working is not for everyone. Open-plan spaces can be noisy, and people whose work involves confidential telephone calls may find them unsuitable unless private rooms are available. Costs can also add up: a full-time desk in a city-centre space can be expensive compared with working from home. Nevertheless, for many workers the combination of flexibility, facilities and social contact makes the shared office an attractive alternative.

passage:
Growing Together: The Benefits of Community Gardens

A  On a former car park between two blocks of flats, rows of raised beds are filled with tomatoes, beans and herbs. A retired engineer is repairing a water tank, while two teenagers are building a compost bin under the guidance of a volunteer. This is one of thousands of community gardens that have been created in towns and cities in recent decades, often on unused land.

B  The most obvious benefit is food. For households with limited incomes, being able to grow fresh vegetables can make a real difference, and many gardens share their harvests with local food banks. Yet research suggests that the social benefits may be at least as important. Gardens bring together people of different ages and backgrounds who might otherwise never meet, and members often describe a strong sense of belonging. In areas with few parks, they also provide green space for relaxation.

C  There is growing evidence that gardening is good for health. Physical work such as digging and carrying provides moderate exercise, and studies have linked regular gardening with lower stress and improved mood. Some doctors now refer patients with mild depression or loneliness to community gardening projects, a practice sometimes called 'social prescribing'.

D  Running a community garden is not without challenges. Many gardens occupy land on temporary agreements and can be closed if the owner decides to build on it. Volunteers may lose interest over time, leaving a small group to do most of the work. Successful gardens tend to have clear rules about responsibilities, regular events that keep members involved, and a good relationship with the local council, which can sometimes offer longer leases or help with water supplies.
question:
Does the following statement agree with the information given in the passage? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
Many community gardens give some of their produce to food banks.
explanation: 第B段落に多くの菜園が収穫をフードバンクと分け合うとあるので TRUE。

passage:
Learning from Experience: Mentoring at Work

A  Starting a new job can be overwhelming. As well as learning the tasks involved, new employees must understand how the organisation works, who makes decisions and what is expected of them, much of which is never written down. To help with this, a growing number of employers run mentoring programmes, in which a less experienced employee is paired with a more experienced colleague who offers guidance and support.

B  A mentor is different from a manager. Managers are responsible for setting targets and assessing performance, whereas mentors usually come from a different team and have no formal authority over the person they support. This independence allows the mentee to discuss concerns, such as difficulties with a colleague or uncertainty about their career, that they might not feel comfortable raising with their manager. Conversations between mentors and mentees are normally kept confidential.

C  The benefits for mentees can be considerable. Studies have found that employees who have a mentor tend to feel more confident, settle into their roles more quickly and are more likely to stay with their employer. Mentoring can be especially valuable for people from groups that are under-represented in senior positions, since it gives them access to advice and professional networks that might otherwise be hard to reach.

D  Mentors benefit too. Many say that explaining their work to someone else helps them to reflect on their own practice, and that they learn a great deal from the fresh perspectives of younger colleagues. In 'reverse mentoring' schemes, the usual roles are deliberately swapped: junior employees help senior managers understand new technology or the experiences of younger customers and staff.

E  Not all mentoring relationships succeed. Problems often arise when the two people meet too rarely, when goals are unclear or when the pairing is simply a poor match. Well-run programmes therefore provide training for mentors, ask both participants to agree on goals at the start and allow either person to end the arrangement without blame if it is not working. Most programmes last between six and twelve months, after which many pairs continue to meet informally.
question:
Does the following statement agree with the information given in the passage? Choose TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN.
Mentors usually have authority to assess their mentees' performance.
explanation: 第B段落でメンターは通常正式な権限を持たないとあるので FALSE。
